procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated the 24th day of March 1950 of the Registrar of Trade Marks in the matter of Registered Trade Mark No. 3815.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Appeal No. 112 of 1950 in the High Court of Judicature at Calcutta. The High Court issued a Judgment and Order dated the 23rd day of August 1951.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Registrar appealed to the Supreme Court under Article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution after the High Court certified that it was a fit case for appeal. The Supreme Court dismissed the respondent's application to rescind the special leave granted to the appellant, citing an initial irregularity in issuing a notice under Order XXXIJ, rule 9 of the Original Side Rules of the Calcutta High Court. The Supreme Court directed the Registrar, Original Side of the Calcutta High Court, to issue a notice under Order XXXrI, rule 9 of the Original Side Rules and instructed the appellants to promptly take steps towards printing and transmitting the record to the Supreme Court.

directions: the respondent company must pav the appellant's costs in this Court and in the High Court

issue.issue_text: Whether the tribunal's power to require a disclaimer is discretionary and must be exercised only for good cause shown, even if the jurisdictional facts under Section 13(a) and (b) are established.

law.fact_text: Under Section 13 of the Trade Marks Act, the power of the tribunal (the Registrar or the Court) to require a disclaimer is discretionary.
law.relevant_text: The exercise of the power conferred on the Registrar by s. 13 of the Trade Marks Act is alwavs a matter of discretion to be exercised, not capriciously or arbitrarilv but, according to sound principles laid down for the exercise of all judicial discretion.

law.fact_text: The jurisdiction to impose a disclaimer only arises after two conditions are met: 1) one of the jurisdictional facts in Section 13(a) or (b) is established, and 2) the tribunal finds that the trademark contains parts to which the proprietor is not entitled to exclusive use.
law.relevant_text: It is only on the establishment of one of the two jurisdictional 'facts that the Registrar's jurisdiction regarding imposition of a disclaimer arises. Before, however. he may exercise his discretion he must find and hold that there are parts or matters included in the trade mark to the exclusive use of which the proprietor is not not entitled and it is only after this finding is arrived at that the Re~istrar becomes entitled to exercise his discretion.

application.fact_text: The Court rejected the argument that the power to require a disclaimer is automatic once the jurisdictional conditions are met.
application.relevant_text: In cause of the argument it was at one time contended that upon the establishment of the requisite jurisdictional fact and upon the finding that the proprietor w~s not entitled to the exclusive use of any particular part or matter contained in the trade mark the Registrar became entitled, without anything more, to require a disclaimer of that oart or matter. This extreme position, however, was not mnintained in the end and it was conceded... that the exercise of the power con-ferrecl on the Registrar by this section always remained a matter of discretion to be exercised.

application.fact_text: The Court determined that merely establishing the jurisdictional facts and the proprietor's lack of exclusive right to a part of the mark is not sufficient to impose a disclaimer.
application.relevant_text: It follows from what has been stated above that the existence of one of the two jurisdictional facts referred to in clauses (a) and (b) of section 13 and the.finding that the trade mark contains parts or matters to the exclusive use of which the proprietor is not entitled does not conclude the matter...

application.fact_text: The Court held that the discretionary power must be exercised only when a good reason or "good cause" for imposing the disclaimer is also established.
application.relevant_text: ...it must further be established that some good reason exists for the imposition of a disclaimer and the tribunal will only exercise the discretionary power for gl'od canse shown.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that even when the jurisdictional facts under Section 13 are established, the tribunal's power to require a disclaimer is not automatic. It is a discretionary power that must be exercised according to sound judicial principles and only for "good cause shown." Therefore, it must be separately established that a good reason exists for imposing the disclaimer before the tribunal can require one.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the tribunal's power to require a disclaimer is discretionary and must be exercised only for good cause shown, even if the jurisdictional facts under Section 13(a) and (b) are established.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (Registrar) argued that the power to impose a disclaimer is a matter of discretion and that this discretion was properly exercised in the case.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (the company) resisted the imposition of a disclaimer, implying they argued that there was no good cause for the tribunal to exercise its discretionary power in this specific instance.

cases.principle: A condition, such as a disclaimer, should only be imposed by a tribunal for 'good cause shewn'. The burden is on establishing a good reason for the condition, rather than on showing a good reason not to impose it, as the object of the legislature was to relieve traders from the necessity of disclaiming.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The finding that a trademark contains parts to which the proprietor is not entitled to exclusive use does not, by itself, necessitate a disclaimer; it must be further established that a good reason exists for its imposition, as the tribunal's power to require a disclaimer is discretionary and must only be exercised for good cause shown.
obiter: The object of the Legislature was to relieve traders from the necessity of disclaiming, and the condition is one for the imposition of which some good reason ought to be established rather than one which ought to be imposed, unless some good reason to the contrary is made out.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The power of the tribunal to require a disclaimer under Section 13 is discretionary and does not automatically follow from the establishment of the jurisdictional facts in clauses (a) and (b). The existence of these jurisdictional facts and a finding that the trademark contains parts to which the proprietor is not entitled to exclusive use only grants the tribunal the jurisdiction to act. The tribunal must then, as a separate step, determine if there is "good cause shown" to exercise its discretion and impose the disclaimer. This discretion must be exercised not capriciously or arbitrarily, but according to sound judicial principles.
legal_tests_applied: The exercise of the power to require a disclaimer is a two-step process: first, one of the two jurisdictional facts in Section 13(a) or (b) must be established, and second, it must be further established that some good reason or 'good cause' exists for the imposition of a disclaimer.

The power conferred on the tribunal is an enabling power, which should only be exercised for good cause shown, rather than being a condition that ought to be imposed unless a good reason to the contrary is made out.
The discretion must be exercised according to sound principles laid down for the exercise of all judicial discretion, not capriciously or arbitrarily.
why_respondent_won: The Registrar's exercise of discretion was found to be proper because it was based on a valid 'good cause': the important consideration of the strong possibility that the proprietor might attempt to expand the operation of its trademark to parts to which it is not entitled.

The High Court erred by interfering with the Registrar's discretion, as it incorrectly concluded that the only reason for the disclaimer was the 'desirability of having a uniform practice' and failed to consider the more substantial reason identified by the Registrar.
policy_considerations: The object of the Legislature was to relieve traders from the necessity of disclaiming, which implies that a disclaimer should be imposed only when a good reason is established.

The possibility of a trademark proprietor attempting to expand the operation of their trademark cannot be ignored or overlooked and is a key factor to be taken into consideration by the tribunal when deciding whether to exercise its discretionary power to require a disclaimer.
